Every `Request`, `Acknowledge`, and `Commit` message must declare the exact subset of degrees of freedom being transferred. The formal transition state machine of @sec-intervention-authority-transitions moves proposal tokens exclusively for those designated channels, and the subsequent `Confirm` phase explicitly annunciates active ownership on each channel back to the operator console. A channel left out of the bitmask may keep its autonomous owner, so the base can keep navigating while the operator takes the arm, but only while the console annunciates that the base is still moving under the policy and the operator's acknowledgment covered that state. Without that annunciation, the commit places the untransferred channel in a certified holding state, such as an active brake hold, rather than letting autonomous execution continue silently. The wet-shrink-wrap collision above is the second rule's case, an untransferred base left running without annunciation.

Explicit channel ownership protocols solve arbitration on the digital bus, but they cannot restore the situational awareness of an out-of-loop human. For this reason, the in-loop and out-of-loop takeovers of @sec-intervention-reaction-drift must be treated as distinct operational states with different timing budgets, the `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_in_str` and `{python} InterventionTakeoverBudget.t_ool_str` that set different request speeds. While gaze tracking can verify where an operator directs their eyes, it cannot verify cognitive comprehension or justify truncating the required takeover latency budget. Local stopping envelopes must remain continuously armed and active, even when the console reports an attentive supervisor. Two field incidents show what happens when either half of this two-layer protection is missing.

In the Tempe, Arizona collision, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) determined that the safety driver was visually distracted by a personal smartphone, identifying operator complacency and inadequate monitoring policies as primary contributing factors [@ntsb2019uber]. The vehicle architecture had disabled automatic emergency braking during testing and relied entirely on the human supervisor to perceive hazards and intervene\index{Tempe fatal collision!operator monitoring}. In the San Francisco Cruise incident, an autonomous vehicle executed an emergency stop after striking a pedestrian who had been thrown into its path by an adjacent human-driven car; however, the onboard planner subsequently initiated an automated pull-over maneuver, dragging the pedestrian beneath the chassis [@quinnemanuel2024cruise]. The Tempe disaster demonstrates why an operator-monitoring contract must always be backed by an autonomous, local stopping envelope capable of bringing the machine to a halt within the remaining sensor clearance, regardless of operator attentiveness. The Cruise incident demonstrates that unexpected physical contact, tactile sensor anomalies, or sudden external force spikes must immediately lock out all motion authority into a verified physical inspection hold, rather than allowing automated post-collision clearing routines to execute.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The Tempe timeline, including the action suppression that withheld emergency braking, is established in @sec-boundary-when-fails.
:::

A human operator's manual command can oppose an active safety barrier without creating a multi-writer conflict on the actuator bus. When an operator commands a manipulator toward a prohibited obstacle, the downstream safety enforcer either projects the trajectory onto the safe half-space or rejects the command entirely, dispatching only the admitted control action to the motor drives. However, the supervisory console must make this active constraint immediately visible to the human. If the interface conceals why the robot has stopped responding, the operator will instinctively command higher control effort or larger joystick displacements, leading to severe command saturation and instability once the constraint clears. Furthermore, when the console incorporates bilateral teleoperation or force-feedback interfaces, system stability depends directly on the passivity-based energy bounds established in @sec-intervention-haptic-passivity; ownership tokens alone cannot prevent feedback oscillations across a physical-virtual coupled loop.

Authority ambiguity also corrupts downstream imitation learning\index{Behavioral cloning}. If the record cannot say who held each channel, interventions are mislabeled as autonomous behavior or the reverse, and a behavioral-cloning policy learns to reproduce the very errors that triggered the takeover. A low offline validation loss cannot catch this, because it only shows that the policy memorized the wrong labels. Causal intervention masking\index{Intervention masking}, developed in @sec-intervention-recovery-eligibility, depends on ownership bits that the authority record stamps at commit time.

\clearpage

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-flight2904-strip
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FLIGHT 2904 GROUND-CONTACT TIMING STRIP (FIGURE GUARD)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: ws-intervention-when-automation-holds-authority-crew-cannot
# │          (ws_flight2904_authority_lockout.svg).
# │
# │ Goal:    Keep the hand-drawn, to-scale strip in step with its source.
# │ Show:    Left-gear contact and the start of wheel braking after right-gear
# │          contact; the strip's time scale.
# │ How:     BFU 1994 report: the left gear touched the runway 9 s after the
# │          right; the wheel brakes began to act about 4 s after the left gear
# │          touched. The SVG places t at x = 190 + 30 px/s; this cell reads the
# │          drawn guide lines back from the file.
# │
# │ Imports: (none)
# │ Exports: (none; guard only)
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import os as _os
import re as _re
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class InterventionFlight2904Strip:
    """Timing values drawn in ws_flight2904_authority_lockout.svg."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_left_gear_s = 9  # category: sourced (bfu1994warsaw)
    t_brake_after_left_s = 4  # category: sourced (bfu1994warsaw, "about 4 seconds")
    x0_px, px_per_s = 190, 30  # category: chosen (drawing scale)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_brake_s = t_left_gear_s + t_brake_after_left_s
    _svg_rel = "images/svg/ws_flight2904_authority_lockout.svg"
    _svg_path = next(_p for _p in (_svg_rel, "books/vol4/14_intervention/" + _svg_rel, "vol4/14_intervention/" + _svg_rel) if _os.path.exists(_p))
    with open(_svg_path) as _f:
        _svg = _f.read()
    _guides = {int(m) for m in _re.findall(r'<line x1="(\d+)" y1="30"', _svg)}

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(_guides == {x0_px + px_per_s * t_left_gear_s, x0_px + px_per_s * t_brake_s}, "flight 2904 strip guides are stale")
    check(f"left gear contact, {t_left_gear_s} s" in _svg, "flight 2904 left-gear label is stale")
    check(f"brakes act, {t_brake_s} s" in _svg, "flight 2904 brake label is stale")
```

::: {#ws-intervention-when-automation-holds-authority-crew-cannot .callout-war-story title="Ground-contact interlocks on flight 2904"}

![](images/svg/ws_flight2904_authority_lockout.svg){fig-alt="To-scale timing strip over fifteen seconds after the right main gear touches down. The right gear is on the ground from time zero; the left gear strut stays uncompressed until 9 seconds. A crew command bar for brakes and reversers runs from touchdown. Ground spoilers and thrust reversers are locked out until 9 seconds and deployed afterward. Wheel brakes show no braking while the wheels aquaplane until 13 seconds, then braking." width=100%}

**Context**: On Lufthansa Flight 2904 at Warsaw, the flight crew executed an approach based on outdated wind reports, encountering an unreported tailwind that caused the aircraft to touch down at high speed far down a waterlogged runway. Upon touchdown, the crew immediately commanded maximum manual braking and deployed thrust reversers, but the aircraft's automated flight-control logic refused to grant deceleration authority [@bfu1994warsaw].

**Mechanism**: Crosswinds and runway hydroplaning delayed the left gear compression: the right main gear made contact 9 s before the left. The aircraft's deceleration interlocks were rigid: ground spoiler deployment required weight-on-wheels shock-strut compression on both main gears **or** wheel spin-up above 72 knots; thrust reversers required weight compression on both main struts; and mechanical wheel braking was locked out until the main wheels achieved synchronized spin-up. Because hydroplaning prevented wheel spin-up and an asymmetric roll angle kept the left strut uncompressed, the control logic determined the aircraft was still airborne. Consequently, the flight computer locked out spoilers and reversers for 9 s and inhibited wheel brakes for even longer.

**Impact**: Wheel braking was inhibited until 13 s after initial touchdown. With braking authority locked out across the primary deceleration zone, the aircraft could not dissipate its kinetic energy along the remaining wet runway. It overran the runway threshold at 72 knots, struck an airport embankment, and caught fire, resulting in two fatalities and total hull loss.

**Response**: Official accident investigators cited the ground-contact interlock logic as a critical contributing cause alongside crew decision-making and delayed meteorological updates. The crew could not override the spoiler and reverser lockouts. The report identifies those design constraints alongside crew actions and incomplete landing-distance guidance; it does not establish that a manual override alone would have prevented the overrun.

**Systems lesson**: Embodied robots share this exact failure topology whenever automated sensor preconditions, such as docking latch checks, wheel-slip traction observers, or ground-contact switches, gate emergency braking or reverse-torque commands issued by human supervisors. Unmodeled wheel slippage or uneven terrain can violate a sensor predicate precisely when deceleration is urgently required. Any control architecture that gates physical actuation behind automated preconditions must satisfy three rules: first, it must immediately annunciate unsatisfied interlocks across the operator console; second, it must explicitly identify the unfulfilled sensor predicate; and third, it must provide a deterministic fallback mode for sensor disagreement. Rather than bypassing safety interlocks blindly, the supervisory architecture must define a certified fallback deceleration path that executes based on conservative, physically verifiable stops.
:::

The formal authority arbiter detailed in @sec-intervention-authority-transitions exists to prevent these failures. Safe embodied control architectures\index{Control architecture} cannot rely on implicit authority handoffs, assumed human vigilance, or ad hoc torque summing on the actuator bus. Evaluating post-incident behavior requires a tamper-evident, channel-by-channel telemetry record captured at every control cycle, with explicit gaps and bounded event timing. The surviving record can help distinguish a safety boundary breach, an invalid token exchange, and electrical noise on a safety bus only to the extent that its independent measurements, capture coverage, and timing bounds separate those events. Its storage path must therefore survive unexpected power interruptions, kernel panics, and real-time scheduling stalls.

## Trustworthy Operational Logs {#sec-intervention-trustworthy-logs}

Consider a robotic arm striking a warehouse racking upright during a supervisory takeover. If the operational log contains an unrecorded gap, investigators cannot determine whether the policy proposed the damaging trajectory, the enforcer admitted it, or the operator received authority too late to intervene. Rigorous incident reconstruction requires two foundational properties: declared loss handling and an operational record engineered to survive physical failure.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-record-baselines
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ VEHICLE EVENT DATA RECORDER BASELINE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-trustworthy-logs, footnote fn-std-edr-baseline.
# │
# │ Goal:    Contrast the regulated vehicle recorder's pre-crash sampling with
# │          the machine's permission tick.
# │ Show:    Part 563 pre-crash window and rate before and after the 2024 rule;
# │          the new sample period in permission ticks.
# │ How:     Window and rate from NHTSA's 2024 final rule (89 FR 102810);
# │          period = 1 / rate; ticks = period / AISLE.t_tick.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import second, millisecond, hertz
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, fmt_count, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class InterventionRecordBaselines:
    """Regulated vehicle pre-crash recording against the permission tick."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    # Source: NHTSA, 49 CFR Part 563 final rule, 89 FR 102810 (2024-12-18).
    # Promotion candidate: literature registry (regulatory recorder baseline).
    edr_old_window = 5 * second  # category: sourced
    edr_old_rate = 2 * hertz  # category: sourced
    edr_new_window = 20 * second  # category: sourced
    edr_new_rate = 10 * hertz  # category: sourced
    # Source: UN Regulation No. 157 (ALKS), para. 8.3.1(d): DSSAD timestamp
    # accuracy +/- 1.0 s. Promotion candidate: literature registry.
    dssad_accuracy = 1.0 * second  # category: sourced
    tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    edr_new_period = (1 / edr_new_rate).to(millisecond)
    edr_ticks = (edr_new_period / tick).to("").magnitude
    dssad_ticks = (dssad_accuracy / tick).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(edr_new_period.magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, f"new recorder sample period: {edr_new_period}")
    check(abs(edr_ticks - 100.0) < 1e-9, f"recorder period in permission ticks: {edr_ticks}")
    check(abs(dssad_ticks - 1000.0) < 1e-9, f"DSSAD accuracy in permission ticks: {dssad_ticks}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    edr_old_window_str = fmt_latency(edr_old_window, unit=second, precision=0)
    edr_old_rate_str = fmt_frequency(edr_old_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    edr_new_window_str = fmt_latency(edr_new_window, unit=second, precision=0)
    edr_new_rate_str = fmt_frequency(edr_new_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    edr_new_period_str = fmt_latency(edr_new_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    edr_ticks_str = fmt_count(edr_ticks, precision=0)
    dssad_accuracy_str = fmt_latency(dssad_accuracy, unit=second, precision=0)
    dssad_ticks_str = fmt_count(dssad_ticks, precision=0)
```

A trustworthy record must capture state on both sides of the causal boundary, paired with independent plant observations.[^fn-std-edr-baseline] Motor phase currents, optical encoder positions, and wrist force-torque measurements provide physical observations distinct from software setpoints, subject to their calibration, bandwidth, and uncertainty bounds. Dispatched commands alone cannot prove delivered actuator torque or establish mechanical collision causality.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ A record of what was proposed, evaluated, dispatched, and measured is the third demand on the permission path established in @sec-boundary-safety-convergence.
:::

[^fn-std-edr-baseline]: **Event Data Recorder Baseline**\index{Event data recorder!sampling baseline}: A passenger-vehicle event data recorder captures `{python} InterventionRecordBaselines.edr_old_window_str` of pre-crash data at `{python} InterventionRecordBaselines.edr_old_rate_str` (expanding from September 2027 to `{python} InterventionRecordBaselines.edr_new_window_str` at `{python} InterventionRecordBaselines.edr_new_rate_str`), which even under the modernized rule yields only one sample per `{python} InterventionRecordBaselines.edr_new_period_str` across `{python} InterventionRecordBaselines.edr_ticks_str` permission ticks [@nhtsa2024edr]. Similarly, the data storage system mandated for automated lane-keeping systems under UN Regulation No. 157 logs system activations, overrides, and transition demands to establish driver attribution, but its timestamps require accuracy only within `{python} InterventionRecordBaselines.dssad_accuracy_str`, or `{python} InterventionRecordBaselines.dssad_ticks_str` permission ticks [@unece2021r157]. Because neither regulatory standard provides the temporal resolution needed to order an intervention against physical contact within a single control cycle, the autonomous machine must maintain its own deterministic, per-tick operational record.

At every cycle, the `{python} InterventionSharedAuthorityScene.permission_rate_str` deterministic control loop records a structured authority and action tuple under declared loss handling. The minimal **evidence tuple**\index{Evidence tuple} takes the form:
$$\langle \MicrocontrollerClockTime, \RecordedAuthorityState, \MechanicalPlantState, \NominalControlCommand, \CertifiedControlAction, \JointTorque, \text{ID}_{\text{operator}}, \RemainingExecutionLease\rangle$$
This tuple records both sides of the proposal-permission boundary. Its command fields are the action taps of @sec-data-four-stream-action-tap taken at intervention time: $\NominalControlCommand$ is the requested or mapped command ($\RequestedActionTap$ or $\MappedCommandTap$, whichever the source emits), $\CertifiedControlAction$ is the enforced command $\EnforcedCommandTap$, and the measured response $\MeasuredResponseTap$ lives in $\MechanicalPlantState$. The fields are:

- $\MicrocontrollerClockTime$ is the monotonic event timestamp recorded in nanoseconds by the safety microcontroller hardware clock, mapped to other subsystem clocks through a qualified clock-conversion method with an explicit error bound. Expressing values in nanosecond units does not imply nanosecond-level inter-device synchronization accuracy.
- $\RecordedAuthorityState$ records the active discrete authority state (`AUTO`, `PEND`, `BLEND`, `MAN`, `FALLBACK`, or `PROTECTIVE`).
- $\MechanicalPlantState$ captures the instantaneous measured plant state, including joint angles, velocities, motor phase currents, and IMU linear accelerations.
- $\NominalControlCommand$ is the proposed plant control setpoint requested by the cognitive policy or human operator console.
- $\CertifiedControlAction$ is the control command admitted by the enforcer, including a feasible CBF-filtered proposal or the selected qualified fallback. Associated event metadata must distinguish admission, modification, and rejection; @sec-enforcement-qp-projection specifies the projection path.
- $\JointTorque$ is the actuator torque command dispatched across the real-time fieldbus to the motor inverters. It is still a command; delivered motor torque can be estimated from the measured phase currents in $\MechanicalPlantState$ using a qualified motor model and explicit uncertainty bounds.
- $\text{ID}_{\text{operator}}$ identifies the authenticated cryptographic entity holding active proposal rights.
- $\RemainingExecutionLease$ records the remaining time on the active execution lease ($\ChunkLease$ or $\ManualLease$, minus the elapsed duration $\MicrocontrollerClockTime - \LeaseRefreshInstant$).

Omitting any element compromises forensic reconstruction. Logging dispatched setpoints $\JointTorque$ without proposals $\NominalControlCommand$ conceals whether the policy commanded an erratic action in the first place. Omitting enforcer output $\CertifiedControlAction$ obscures whether the safety barrier modified the requested trajectory. Omitting $\RemainingExecutionLease$ hides whether authority had already lapsed into a fallback mode when a command was evaluated. Chained with cryptographic integrity proofs and clock-synchronization metadata, these tuples form the per-tick half of the authority record that @sec-intervention-authority-log specifies.

Three architectural requirements ensure that logged tuples serve as reliable forensic evidence:

First, timestamps must date physical events rather than software handling. A software interrupt handler that samples the clock only after being scheduled records its own execution delay rather than the event time. Under variable scheduling jitter and interrupt latency, this delay can easily invert the apparent chronological order of an intervention command and a mechanical contact. Protective inputs and fieldbus ingress packets must therefore be timestamped directly at the hardware boundary through timer edge capture and network controller hardware counters. When clock-conversion error, sensor exposure windows, and sampling intervals overlap between two events, the log must explicitly record their relative order as indistinguishable rather than asserting an unverified sequence.

Second, the storage pipeline must be strictly tiered by guarantee level. Minimal evidence tuples stream to a bounded ring buffer in non-volatile memory on the safety microcontroller. The serialized tuple size multiplied by the control tick rate sets a continuous write bandwidth that hardware qualification tests must prove the device sustains under all operating regimes, with buffer overflows explicitly flagged rather than silently dropped. High-bandwidth perception streams, including camera frames, point clouds, and policy internal activations, flow to a best-effort buffer on the primary host. This high-volume traffic is never permitted to contend for the safety microcontroller's memory or bus bandwidth.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The multi-camera ingestion rate that this best-effort buffer must absorb is established in @sec-data-telemetry-ingestion-storage.
:::

Third, loss must be declared explicitly. When buffer exhaustion or bus stalls occur, the logger must record a missing entry or overwritten frame as a declared gap in the evidence, never as an implied safe pass.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-pre-trigger-window
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRE-TRIGGER LOGGING WINDOW
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-trustworthy-logs, the pre-trigger paragraph.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the frozen pre-trigger window from the sourced takeover time.
# │ Show:    The design out-of-loop takeover and the window it sets.
# │ How:     AISLE.pre_trigger_window, the design takeover rounded up to whole
# │          seconds (the same window @sec-data-intervention-recovery uses).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import second
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class InterventionPreTriggerWindow:
    """Pre-trigger window that reaches back past the design takeover."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_ool = AISLE.t_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: derived (sourced p90 take-over time + transport)
    t_pre = AISLE.pre_trigger_window  # category: derived

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    headroom = (t_pre - t_ool).to(second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t_pre >= t_ool, "The window must reach back past the design takeover.")
    check(abs(t_pre.to(second).magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, f"pre-trigger window: {t_pre}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_ool_str = fmt_latency(t_ool, unit=second, precision=1)
    t_pre_str = fmt_latency(t_pre, unit=second, precision=0)
```

Upon receiving an intervention trigger, such as an operator takeover command, an emergency stop assertion, or an enforcer barrier violation, the logger freezes a configured **pre-trigger window** ($\PreTriggerWindowDuration =$ `{python} InterventionPreTriggerWindow.t_pre_str`) and transitions to recording a dedicated post-trigger segment. The pre-trigger duration matches the `{python} InterventionPreTriggerWindow.t_ool_str` design out-of-loop takeover latency characterized in @sec-intervention-reaction-drift, rounded up to whole seconds. This window preserves the design takeover interval, but policy divergence may begin before the operator notices it, so its duration alone does not establish that the complete causal chain remains in the log. Operational sites that measure longer takeover tails must lengthen $\PreTriggerWindowDuration$ accordingly. Overwritten frames or dropped samples within this interval remain declared gaps in the evidence. @Sec-data-intervention-recovery uses this same window as its lookback horizon, searching it for the divergence point $\DivergenceInstant$ and detailing why learner-visited states during drift are essential for offline policy training; the authority record provides the cryptographic ownership stamps that allow the training pipeline to distinguish unprivileged policy proposals from enforcer interventions and operator overrides.

Finally, the operational record must reveal any subsequent tampering or truncation. Each entry carries a keyed cryptographic link over its predecessor,[^fn-linked-hash-chain] while periodic authenticated anchors are written to replay-protected storage located outside the logger's primary write path. Rewritable non-volatile storage with authenticated writes satisfies this requirement, avoiding the need for dedicated write-once media. Under this design, investigators can determine exactly which log prefix each anchor authenticates, verify that cryptographic keys and anchors remained in trusted custody, and flag any unanchored tail or missing block as a declared gap. Hardware-level tamper resistance and loss declaration protect record integrity and expose missing evidence; they do not establish that a sensor reading is accurate. To serve post-incident reconstruction and downstream policy training, however, these raw evidence streams must be bound into a formal, machine-checkable artifact: the authority record.

[^fn-linked-hash-chain]: **Linked Hash Chains**\index{Hash chain!linked timestamping}: @haber1991time proposed linking each timestamp to the cryptographic hash of its predecessor, ensuring that no historical record can be backdated or inserted without invalidating every subsequent link. The authority record inherits both this tamper-evident property and its limit, since an adversary possessing the signing keys and complete control over the storage device can recompute the entire chain. To protect against retroactive tampering, commitment anchors must be mirrored to an independent, replay-protected storage domain outside the logger's mutable write path.

## The Authority Record {#sec-intervention-authority-log}

When an incident investigator asks, weeks after an abrupt blocked-aisle takeover, which entity drove the mobile base as it neared the rack end, the machine's recorded telemetry provides evidence bounded by its capture coverage, clock alignment, independent plant measurements, and trusted custody. The **authority record**\index{Authority record!definition} bridges real-time supervisory arbitration with downstream verification and release claims. To establish this audit trail, the authority record consumes two upstream contracts. From the enforcement record of @sec-enforcement-telemetry, it ingests the rungs of the fallback ladder so that every logged fallback explicitly identifies the rung executed by the permission path. From the placement record of @sec-placement-hardware-allocation, it incorporates the permission path's declared timing bounds and bus arbitration settings, which every operator command also crosses, together with the placement record's loaded-test field, which stays empty until verification fills it. The record shows who held each channel at each tick; it does not show who decided the speed, the staffing, or the operating domain that put the machine there.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The record of who decided that the machine could be in that situation at all, with a named owner for each decision, is developed in @sec-responsibility-approval-record.
:::

To these upstream contracts, the authority record adds two deliverables of its own. The static authority manifest translates the capability matrix of @sec-intervention-human-authority into a machine-checkable contract. It binds every actuator channel to its authorized actors, operational preconditions, preemption tiers, and transition deadlines, and the safety microcontroller verifies and seals this manifest before the actuator drivers energize. Complementing the manifest, the record's per-tick log\index{Authority record!per-tick log} forms an independent stream that records, for every control cycle, which entity held kinetic authority alongside the commands proposed, admitted, and dispatched, paired with independently measured physical response. In this stream, a missing cycle registers as an explicit communication or capture gap rather than an implied pass. The static manifest establishes the legal rules of interaction, while the per-tick log supports checking recorded runtime adherence under the capture, synchronization, custody, and declared-gap assumptions of @sec-intervention-trustworthy-logs.

### The static authority manifest and capability binding {#sec-intervention-manifest-binding}

The static authority manifest defines the ground truth against which all recorded arbitration decisions are evaluated. Loading and cryptographically sealing the manifest during system initialization binds every subsequent event to the permissions and physical limits in force at boot. It specifies every permitted interaction as a verifiable contract between the physical platform and potential command sources. Each entry delineates a distinct physical authority domain using a hardware actuator mask, an authorized entity class (such as a local physical operator, a remote teleoperation console, an autonomous trajectory policy, or an emergency stop loop), and an integer **preemption tier**\index{Preemption tier}. Before any command vector enters the actuation pipeline, the permission path verifies the sender's cryptographic role credentials against this manifest. Over the network, an operator's command arrives as an `OPERATOR` payload under the same proposal header, carrying the operator's role, the requested channel mask, the command vector, a monotonically increasing nonce, and a keyed authentication tag.

In addition to credential validation, each manifest entry enforces four operational invariants on its assigned channel:

1. *Single-writer mutual exclusion*: Hardware access controls guarantee that exactly one entity writes to an actuator channel at any given instant.
2. *Execution lease duration ($\ManualLease$)*: For human operators, the lease defines the maximum tolerable silence before the enforcer revokes authority and triggers a state-dependent fallback.
3. *Command rate ceiling ($\CommandRateCeiling$)*: A hardware slew limit caps how rapidly a requested command vector may change between successive cycles, preventing abrupt step inputs.
4. *Bumpless blending duration ($\BlendingTransitionWindow$)*: A transition window enforces a $\Glyph{C}^2$ continuous authority transfer ramp that preserves the kinodynamic feasibility bounds established in @sec-planning-kinodynamic-feasibility, requiring a qualified executable profile and a feasible state-matched fallback at every transition state if communication severs. The fallback depends on surviving sensing, controller, and energy premises; duration and continuity alone do not establish it.

### Per-tick evidence tuples and the fault injection suite {#sec-intervention-evidence-tuples}

Every entry in the authority record's per-tick log instantiates the evidence tuple defined in @sec-intervention-trustworthy-logs, expanding on fields that the general tuple leaves implicit: the specific actuator channels governed by the arbitration decision, the ladder rung of any active `FALLBACK`, the root cause of any preemption, the instantaneous blend factor $\BumplessTransferBlend(\TimeInstant)$ of the enforcer-managed profile, and a cryptographic hash link to the preceding log block authenticated through the platform's protected anchoring scheme. The versioned static manifest supplies the decoding context, specifying physical units, field serialization order, clock synchronization mappings with their associated error bounds, credential validation rules, and hardware access control masks.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Byte layout:** The operator payload's and the authority record's fields, types, and offsets are given in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-authority.
:::

Verification draws its test inputs from the static manifest and its evidence from the event schema. The manifest's `authority_claims` field hands @sec-verification-forward-analysis four authority rules by identifier, each of which becomes a hardware-in-the-loop fault case on the machine:

- **A1.** Exactly one qualified enforcer output path writes each actuator channel. Source arbitration and hardware access controls prevent a second sender from bypassing that path while the policy and remote assistant both propose commands; successful bus arbitration alone does not satisfy this claim.
- **A2.** No lower-tier source bypasses an active higher-tier source or the independent permission check. An autonomous policy proposal during `MAN` is ignored, and an assistant command that opposes the enforcer's admitted barrier limit is clamped or rejected.
- **A3.** An unacknowledged handover or stalled manual lease decays authority by $\HandoverTimeout$ of @sec-intervention-clearance-deadlines, initiating controlled fallback by the earlier of the configured lease ceiling and the clearance-derived deadline of @eq-intervention-latest-fallback. This clearance deadline has a partial-budget upper bound of `{python} InterventionAssistantSession.t_latest_in_str` at the `{python} InterventionAssistantSession.v_in_str` slow-down before an in-loop takeover, and `{python} InterventionAssistantSession.t_latest_str` for a handover requested by the policy at the `{python} InterventionAssistantSession.v_aisle_str` aisle speed. Both values represent additional-delay allocations in the capture-origin budget. The runtime deadline evaluates the actual event history and future delay budgets without double-charging for elapsed capture-to-admission transit.
- **A4.** The enforcer rejects replayed `veto_path`, `manual_drive`, or `accept_item` packets, and packets with invalid authentication tags or expired sequence counters, without modifying still-valid channel authority. It logs each rejection in the evidence tuple while allowing the active lease to age normally.

These authority rules turn the event log into a checkable contract. The same synchronized hardware timestamps also mark which controller generated each segment of an intervention trajectory, and that separation must exist before any segment can serve as a training target for imitation learning.

### Causal masking and recovery eligibility {#sec-intervention-recovery-eligibility}

The curation rules of @sec-data-intervention-recovery decide which logged samples may train a policy. Drift commands are quarantined, drift states are relabeled only by an automated expert, and only stabilized, reviewed recovery is admitted. Each rule keys on a timestamp that the authority record supplies, so a logging system that records intervention episodes for downstream policy retraining must preserve controller ownership, target meaning, and declared sample eligibility. This chapter's conservative direct-imitation policy applies **causal intervention masking**\index{Causal intervention masking} to that record. Its optimization objective over recorded trajectories is formulated as:
$$\MaskedImitationLoss(\ModelParameters) = \mathbb{E}_{(\MechanicalPlantState, \ImitationTargetCommand, \CausalInterventionMask) \sim \MaskedImitationDataset} \left[ \sum_{k=0}^{\BehaviorCloningHorizon} \CausalInterventionMask(\ControlSampleIndex) \cdot \ell\left(\Policy(\MechanicalPlantState_k), \ImitationTargetCommand(\ControlSampleIndex)\right) \right]$$ {#eq-intervention-causal-masking-loss}
where $\ell(\Policy(\MechanicalPlantState_k), \ImitationTargetCommand(\ControlSampleIndex))$ denotes the policy prediction loss (such as mean squared error across action chunks or score-matching denoising loss for diffusion policies), $\CausalInterventionMask(\ControlSampleIndex) \in \{0, 1\}$ is a binary causal mask, and $\ImitationTargetCommand(\ControlSampleIndex)$ is the supervised training target, with the mask and target at each sample evaluated at that sample's logged hardware timestamp. The target carries its own symbol because it is not the admitted command $\CertifiedControlAction$ of the evidence tuple; in each interval it is chosen from the logged fields, or supplied by an expert, as the interval list below states. Constructing the training dataset $\MaskedImitationDataset$ requires selective transformation rather than wholesale ingestion of raw telemetry. While every logged state preserves its chronological position in the trajectory, its supervision target $\ImitationTargetCommand(\TimeInstant)$ and mask $\CausalInterventionMask(\TimeInstant)$ depend on the physical regime of the recording interval. As a result, the command dispatched to the hardware is not necessarily the training target. Deterministic authority transitions stamped by the safety microcontroller establish controller ownership, while empirical stabilization criteria, task validity checks, and the availability of expert labels determine which samples receive $\CausalInterventionMask(\TimeInstant) = 1$.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-learning-evidence
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ INTERVAL LENGTHS FROM THE HUMAN-IN-THE-LOOP LITERATURE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-recovery-eligibility, interval 3 and the
# │          paragraph before @tbl-14-intervention-learning.
# │
# │ Goal:    Set two published interval lengths against the machine's own.
# │ Show:    Sirius's fixed pre-intervention window (robot actions and time);
# │          the design out-of-loop takeover as a multiple of it; the time
# │          drivers needed to stabilize lateral control after resuming it,
# │          as a multiple of the pre-trigger window.
# │ How:     Literature constants (below) against AISLE.t_takeover_out_of_loop
# │          and AISLE.pre_trigger_window.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import second
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_count, fmt_multiple, fmt_time_range, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class InterventionLearningEvidence:
    """Published interval lengths against the machine's takeover and window."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    # Source: Liu et al., RSS 2023 (Sirius), Sec. IV: pre-intervention class of
    # l = 15 robot actions, matching an observed operator reaction time of 2 s.
    # Promotion candidate: literature registry.
    sirius_actions = 15  # category: sourced
    sirius_window = 2 * second  # category: sourced
    # Source: Merat et al., TR Part F 27 (2014), abstract: 35-40 s to stabilize
    # lateral control after resuming manual driving. Promotion candidate.
    merat_lo = 35 * second  # category: sourced
    merat_hi = 40 * second  # category: sourced
    t_ool = AISLE.t_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: derived (sourced)
    t_pre = AISLE.pre_trigger_window  # category: derived

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_ool_over_sirius = (t_ool / sirius_window).to("").magnitude
    merat_over_pre = (merat_lo / t_pre).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_ool_over_sirius - 2.23) < 0.01, f"design takeover over Sirius window: {t_ool_over_sirius}")
    check(abs(merat_over_pre - 7.0) < 1e-9, f"stabilization over pre-trigger window: {merat_over_pre}")
    check(t_ool > sirius_window, "The design takeover must outlast the fixed window.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    sirius_actions_str = fmt_count(sirius_actions, precision=0)
    sirius_window_str = fmt_latency(sirius_window, unit=second, precision=0)
    t_ool_over_sirius_mult_str = fmt_multiple(t_ool_over_sirius, precision=1)
    merat_stable_str = fmt_time_range(merat_lo, merat_hi, unit=second)
    merat_over_pre_mult_str = fmt_multiple(merat_over_pre, precision=0)
    t_pre_str = fmt_latency(t_pre, unit=second, precision=0)
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_intervention_owner_strip.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Unscaled strip of four cells labeled drift, blend, re-orient, and stable. The first three cells are outlined and marked M equals 0; the last is filled and marked M equals 1, under a bracket labeled trains."}

*One intervention, four intervals; only validated, stabilized recovery trains directly as a human demonstration.*
:::

A supervisory intervention does not occur as a single monolithic demonstration. Instead, it spans four distinct physical intervals along the execution timeline:

1. **Compounding policy drift ($\DivergenceInstant \le \TimeInstant < \CommitmentInstant$)**: The autonomous policy $\Policy$ drifts away from the expert state distribution, accumulating compounding errors while the human supervisor perceives the anomaly, orients, and decides to intervene (the pre-commit latency modeled in @eq-intervention-reaction-floor).
   - *Masking policy*: The autonomous proposals $\NominalControlCommand(\TimeInstant)$ executed during this drift are quarantined from training targets. Without an external expert label, the system sets $\CausalInterventionMask(\TimeInstant) = 0$.
   - *Relabeling*: The *learner-visited states* $\MechanicalPlantState(\TimeInstant)$ remain in the log for the corrective aggregation of @sec-data-intervention-recovery, whose relabeling rule accepts only an automated expert's labels. A drift state therefore enters training with $\CausalInterventionMask(\TimeInstant) = 1$ and target $\ImitationTargetCommand(\TimeInstant) = \pi^*(\MechanicalPlantState_t)$ only when such an expert, for example an omniscient trajectory planner with privileged simulation state, supplies the correction.
2. **Atomic handover and enforcer blend ($\CommitmentInstant \le \TimeInstant < \CommitmentInstant + \BlendingTransitionWindow$)**: The safety microcontroller latches the channel endpoints and computes a $\Glyph{C}^2$ continuous smoothstep trajectory between controllers.
   - *Masking policy*: The system sets $\CausalInterventionMask(\TimeInstant) = 0$ unconditionally. Dispatched setpoints $\ControlCommand(\TimeInstant)$ during this window are synthetic interpolation splines generated by the enforcer's deterministic quintic polynomial profile. Because they reflect neither learned neural policy intent nor human cognitive demonstration, training on this interval would condition the network to emit open-loop kinematic ramps detached from environmental feedback.
3. **Operator re-orientation and hunting ($\CommitmentInstant + \BlendingTransitionWindow \le \TimeInstant < \OperatorStabilizationInstant$)**: Upon receiving the active manual lease ($\ManualLease$), the operator experiences neuromuscular latency, visual parallax, and control re-orientation, producing high-jerk, oscillatory corrections while regaining situational awareness.
   - *Masking policy*: The system enforces $\CausalInterventionMask(\TimeInstant) = 0$. Bainbridge documented this control hunting directly. An operator whose active manual skill has lapsed during passive monitoring makes abrupt step corrections, oscillating around the setpoint before settling into smooth tracking [@bainbridge1983ironies]. Control stabilization often takes significantly longer than the physical handover itself. In driving simulator studies, operators resuming control from automated systems required approximately `{python} InterventionLearningEvidence.merat_stable_str` before their lateral steering stabilized [@merat2014transition], at least `{python} InterventionLearningEvidence.merat_over_pre_mult_str` the length of the machine's `{python} InterventionLearningEvidence.t_pre_str` pre-trigger window. Consequently, post-trigger masking cannot rely on a fixed time constant; logging systems must evaluate empirical stabilization criteria. Discarding these initial frames prevents hesitation and oscillatory hunting from corrupting the imitation buffer. This exclusion involves an engineering trade-off, because interval 3 also contains the operator's initial corrective inputs, which certain human-gated methods retain (@tbl-14-intervention-learning). The enforcer marks the stabilization boundary $\OperatorStabilizationInstant$ only after tracking error and command slew have remained within calibrated limits for a declared dwell interval. Later violations mask the affected samples again. The limits are:
   $$\lVert \TakeoverTrackingError(\TimeInstant) \rVert \le \StabilizationErrorThreshold \quad \text{and} \quad \lVert \HumanCommandRate(\TimeInstant) \rVert \le \StabilizationSlewCeiling.$$
   Here, the parameter $\StabilizationSlewCeiling$ denotes a channel-specific slew ceiling, representing an acceleration derivative (jerk) only when the underlying command vector represents acceleration.
4. **Stabilized expert recovery ($\TimeInstant \ge \OperatorStabilizationInstant$)**: The operator executes coherent, task-directed recovery maneuvers once measured control metrics stabilize. Smooth motion alone does not validate a recovery; the episode must also satisfy formal task-completion criteria before its samples qualify as expert targets.
   - *Masking policy*: The system sets $\CausalInterventionMask(\TimeInstant) = 1$ with imitation target $\ImitationTargetCommand(\TimeInstant) = \HumanControlCommand(\TimeInstant)$ exclusively for stabilized segments that pass task-validity review. All other telemetry frames remain masked from direct imitation, so this interval is the only post-takeover segment the curation rules admit as expert recovery data.

Feeding unsegmented telemetry directly into behavioral cloning or diffusion policies injects synthetic enforcer ramps and operator control transients into the training distribution. The causal mask $\CausalInterventionMask(\TimeInstant)$ and target vector $\ImitationTargetCommand(\TimeInstant)$ use the commit and state timestamps recorded by the safety microcontroller to enforce controller ownership boundaries, bounded by hardware clock synchronization and sampling limits.

The binary causal mask represents the most conservative member of a broader algorithmic spectrum. Contemporary human-in-the-loop learning methods treat interventions in fundamentally different ways: as direct state labels, as importance weights over surrounding trajectories, or as negative reinforcement signals indicating policy failure. @Tbl-14-intervention-learning maps five representative paradigms onto these four operational intervals. For instance, Human-Gated DAgger (HG-DAgger) grants the human supervisor full authority upon takeover and aggregates only the human's executed commands, leaving interval 1 unmasked but unlabeled [@kelly2019hgdagger]. Sirius generalizes $\CausalInterventionMask(\TimeInstant)$ by assigning categorical importance weights across sample classes; it assigns zero weight to a fixed pre-intervention window while upweighting human recovery trajectories [@liu2023sirius]. Specifically, Sirius sizes its pre-intervention window to `{python} InterventionLearningEvidence.sirius_actions_str` robot actions (approximately `{python} InterventionLearningEvidence.sirius_window_str`), derived from observed human reaction times. While Sirius fixes this window a priori, the authority record timestamps the commit and supports reconstruction of the drift interval once $\DivergenceInstant$ is identified from the retained evidence, a duration that the out-of-loop takeover budget of @sec-intervention-reaction-drift shows can be `{python} InterventionLearningEvidence.t_ool_over_sirius_mult_str` longer. Meanwhile, Reinforcement Learning from Intervention Feedback (RLIF) eliminates the assumption of human optimality altogether, treating the intervention event as a negative reward penalty within an off-policy reinforcement learning framework [@luo2024rlif]. Similarly, Human-in-the-Loop Sample-Efficient Robot Learning (HIL-SERL) incorporates human interventions as targeted correction buffers for real-world reinforcement learning [@luo2025hilserl]. Finally, RECAP, which trains the $\pi^{*}_{0.6}$ vision-language-action model, blends autonomous rollouts, teleoperated interventions, and demonstrations using advantage conditioning, explicitly labeling human takeover corrections as positive-advantage actions [@physicalintelligence2025recap].

| Method (year)                 | What the intervention becomes                    | Interval 1 (policy drift)                     | Interval 3 (re-orientation)           | Needs from the authority record        |
|:------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|
| Causal mask (this chapter)    | Boundary between owners                          | Excluded unless an automated expert labels it | Excluded until measured stabilization | Commit, blend end, stabilization times |
| HG-DAgger (2019)              | Label: human commands while in control           | Not labeled                                   | Kept with the human's commands        | Owner per sample                       |
| Sirius (2023)                 | Weight per sample class                          | Fixed pre-intervention window, weight zero    | Kept, upweighted                      | Commit time; window measured to it     |
| RLIF (2024)                   | Reward: the takeover itself is a penalty         | Kept; the takeover penalizes it               | Human samples added to the data       | Commit time as the reward event        |
| HIL-SERL (2025)               | Correction data for a reinforcement learner      | Kept as the learner's own experience          | Kept as correction data               | Owner per sample                       |
| RECAP, $\pi^{*}_{0.6}$ (2025) | Correction marked as a positive-advantage action | Kept; a value function scores it              | Kept, marked positive                 | Owner per sample; episode outcome      |

: **Human-in-the-loop learning methods as of 2026, placed on the four intervals**: Every method needs the ownership boundary the authority record holds; they differ in what the intervention becomes and in which intervals they train on. None trains on the enforcer's blend as a demonstration. Entries summarize each method's published design [@kelly2019hgdagger; @liu2023sirius; @luo2024rlif; @luo2025hilserl; @physicalintelligence2025recap]; a later edition should refresh the list. {#tbl-14-intervention-learning tbl-colwidths="[17,24,21,19,19]"}

Underlying architectural mechanisms outlast individual learning frameworks. Every method must resolve three fundamental systems questions: which entity held write authority over each sample, whether an intervention represents a supervised label, an importance weight, or an external reward, and which physical intervals are admitted into optimization. Answering these questions requires an unambiguous ownership boundary that downstream training pipelines cannot infer from trajectory kinematics alone. Logging this boundary at commit time grounds dataset curation directly in hardware truth. Furthermore, fleet-level reliability metrics, such as the rate of interventions per operating hour, derive directly from this audit trail.

When establishing the safety case for operational certification, @sec-release-argument-plant-alignment evaluates the authority record as direct evidence for one of the release argument's claims, the claim that runtime authority transfers conform to rules A1 through A4 (labeled C6 in @tbl-16-cae-scorecard). An operational safety audit examines these formal constraints alongside implementation evidence, fault-injection test coverage, and the validated operating envelope. The certification dossier pairs the static authority manifest with the physical plant measurements demanded by @sec-intervention-bumpless-transfer and hardware-in-the-loop execution traces that demonstrate an unbroken audit trail. Physical plant telemetry remains essential because a command handover that is mathematically valid at the communication bus can still slip wheels on a slick surface or violently shift a loaded tote rack. Preemption latencies captured in these traces represent empirical percentiles of the tested distribution rather than theoretical worst-case bounds.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The distinction between an empirical latency percentile and a response-time bound is established in @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses.
:::

::: {#chk-intervention-authority-evidence .callout-checkpoint title="Authority evidence and causal masks"}

The authority record is useful twice, once to an investigator and once to a learner, and both uses depend on the same ownership timestamps.

- [ ] **Evidence tuple**: Can you name the incident question that becomes unanswerable when the log drops $\NominalControlCommand$, when it drops $\CertifiedControlAction$, and when it drops $\RemainingExecutionLease$?
- [ ] **Interval masks**: For one takeover, can you assign $\CausalInterventionMask(\TimeInstant)$ and $\ImitationTargetCommand(\TimeInstant)$ to each of the four intervals and name the logged event that bounds each?
- [ ] **Sample count estimate**: An out-of-loop takeover commits `{python} InterventionPreTriggerWindow.t_ool_str` after the divergence, and the arm then blends for `{python} InterventionBlendBudget.arm_budget_str`. At the `{python} InterventionBlendBudget.tick_str` permission tick, can you estimate how many logged ticks fall in intervals 1 and 2, and how many of them may train an imitation policy when no automated expert is available?
- [ ] **Fixed windows**: Can you explain what a fixed `{python} InterventionLearningEvidence.sirius_window_str` pre-intervention window misclassifies for a takeover that took the design out-of-loop time?

:::

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-intervention-fallacies-pitfalls}

Flipping a bit in an authority register does not complete a safe supervisory handover\index{Handover!authority register}. A real-time physical AI system must preserve its dynamic stopping margin\index{Safety!stopping margin} and protective enforcement functions\index{Enforcement!transfer boundaries} throughout every stage of transfer. Furthermore, downstream imitation learning pipelines cannot treat intervention logs as unblemished expert recoveries\index{Imitation learning!expert recovery} without explicit causal filtering. When systems fail in deployment, the breakdown almost always traces back to one of four subtle architectural traps.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-fixed-window-pitfall
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ONE FIXED ACKNOWLEDGMENT WINDOW AT TWO SPEEDS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-fallacies-pitfalls, the fixed-timeout pitfall.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that one configured window fits at the crawl and overruns at
# │          the aisle speed.
# │ Show:    Travel during the window and the overrun at 1.3 m/s; the spare
# │          and T_latest at the out-of-loop crawl.
# │ How:     Finished stopping budget (jerk-limited resident stop, all
# │          overheads) at each speed, the window added to tau_delay.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import meter, second, millimeter, millisecond
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_stop_distance
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class InterventionFixedWindowPitfall:
    """A configured acknowledgment window judged against the budget at two speeds."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    v_crawl = AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"]  # category: derived (stipulated jerk bound)
    overhead = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: illustrative / chosen
    window = InterventionTimeoutBudget.config  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    def _budget(speed, tau, a, j, ovh):
        return (speed * tau + calc_scurve_stop_distance(speed, a, j) + ovh).to(millimeter)

    budget = _budget(v, tau_delay, a_brake, j_brake, overhead)
    travel = (v * window).to(millimeter)
    overrun = (budget + travel - d_clear).to(millimeter)
    spare_crawl = (d_clear - _budget(v_crawl, tau_delay, a_brake, j_brake, overhead)).to(millimeter)
    t_latest_crawl = (spare_crawl / v_crawl).to(millisecond)
    # Stop with the window waited out, at each speed (margin figure).
    d_stop = (budget + travel).to(millimeter)
    d_stop_crawl = (d_clear - spare_crawl + v_crawl * window).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(budget.magnitude - 968.99) < 5e-3, f"finished budget at the aisle speed: {budget}")
    # margin_fixed_window_stop_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 500 ms, 1619 mm, 307 mm, 1100 mm
    check(round(d_stop.magnitude) == 1619 and round(d_stop_crawl.magnitude) == 307, f"window stops: {d_stop}, {d_stop_crawl}")
    check(
        round(window.to(millisecond).magnitude) == 500 and round(d_clear.to(millimeter).magnitude) == 1100, "window and clear distance in the fig-alt"
    )
    check(abs(v_crawl.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.15) < 1e-9, f"crawl speed in the fig-alt: {v_crawl}")
    check(overrun.magnitude > 0, "The window must overrun the clear distance at the aisle speed.")
    check(t_latest_crawl > window, "The same window must fit at the crawl.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_crawl_str = fmt_velocity(v_crawl, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    window_str = fmt_latency(window, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    travel_str = fmt_length(travel, unit=meter, precision=2)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    overrun_str = fmt_length(overrun, unit=meter, precision=2)
    t_latest_crawl_str = fmt_latency(t_latest_crawl, unit=second, precision=1)
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_fixed_window_stop_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two bars of stopping distance with a 500-millisecond acknowledgment window waited out: 1.62 meters at 1.3 meters per second, crossing a red dashed limit at the 1.10 meter rack-end clearance, and 0.31 meters at 0.15 meters per second, well inside it."}

*One `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.window_str` window overruns at aisle speed and idles at a crawl.*
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Treating human takeover timeout as a static time delay rather than a dynamic spatial stopping budget.*

Consider a mobile manipulator that initiates a takeover request at its operational `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.v_str` aisle speed under a statically configured `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.window_str` acknowledgment window\index{Handover!takeover request}. If the controller waits out that full window before commanding brakes, the vehicle covers `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.travel_str` of unbraked travel. When combined with the jerk-limited resident stop profile and actuator execution overheads, the total stopping distance ends `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.overrun_str` beyond the `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.d_clear_str` rack-end clearance, causing a physical collision. Conversely, at an out-of-loop crawl speed of `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.v_crawl_str`, that same window consumes negligible distance, leaving `{python} InterventionFixedWindowPitfall.t_latest_crawl_str` of margin before fallback braking must begin. The wait costs travel in proportion to speed, and the stop that follows grows with its square, so a timeout that leaves ample response time at a crawl overruns the clear distance at aisle speed. Real-time supervisory handovers cannot treat human response intervals as fixed wall-clock durations; the permissible wait time must be computed dynamically from instantaneous velocity, remaining obstacle clearance, and validated brake deceleration envelopes, initiating autonomous fallback\index{Handover!autonomous fallback} the moment the remaining clearance matches the required stopping profile.

**A supervisory timeout is not a static timer; it is a dynamically bounded spatial margin that must fit the instantaneous stopping budget.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** On every control cycle, evaluate the instantaneous obstacle clearance against a complete stopping budget composed solely of future sensing delays, brake actuation lag, and jerk-limited deceleration. Dynamically recompute a candidate absolute deadline, anchored to a consistent time origin, from @eq-intervention-latest-fallback, which gives the longest wait whose delay travel and stop suffix still fit inside the remaining clearance. If a newly calculated deadline is earlier than the currently active deadline, tighten the expiration threshold immediately; never extend or restart an active countdown based on optimistic recalculations. Account for sensor pipeline latency consistently, and do not subtract historical capture-to-enforcement delay from clearance measurements that have already physically reflected that travel. If supervisory acknowledgment does not arrive before the deadline expires, immediately trigger the validated autonomous fallback brake sequence.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Human manual takeover should bypass automated safety barriers and grant unconstrained, open-ended actuator authority.*

When a remote operator takes manual control of a mobile manipulator to steer it around an unexpected obstacle, the chosen steering commands might vector the chassis directly toward a warehouse rack upright. Granting manual control alters only the origin of proposed motion setpoints; it cannot alter chassis momentum, tire-floor friction coefficients, or environmental obstacle boundaries. The low-level safety enforcer\index{Enforcement!manual override} must therefore evaluate human manual proposals against the formal admissible motion set\index{Safety!admissible motion} on every cycle. If the operator commands a trajectory that risks collision or dynamic instability, the enforcer projects the command onto the nearest safe, kinodynamically feasible trajectory. If no safe trajectory exists within the admissible envelope, the enforcer rejects the proposal entirely and triggers an immediate autonomous fallback. Manual intervention grants the operator authority to guide high-level intent, but mechanical stresses, obstacle clearance, and brake margins remain hard physical constraints enforced at the joint actuator\index{Hardware!actuator boundary} boundary.

Furthermore, manual intervention must operate under strictly bounded, perishable leases rather than open-ended authority grants. Transient wireless packet loss or operator distraction can easily leave stale velocity vectors active in flight. To prevent uncommanded runaway motion, every intervention session requires a cryptographically renewed manual lease calibrated to the active operational mode's stopping reserve. In this warehouse aisle scenario, the system enforces a `{python} InterventionTimeoutBudget.manual_lease_str` manual lease. If periodic, authenticated heartbeat renewals fail to arrive before the lease expires, the safety microcontroller immediately revokes proposal authority and executes an autonomous fallback stop independently of host software or operator intervention.

**Manual intervention transfers the authority to propose setpoints, but never the authority to bypass physical barrier certificates or operate on stale communication.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Channel all teleoperation and manual override inputs through the enforcer's control barrier certificates and kinodynamic clamping filters. When an operator command exceeds dynamic rollover thresholds, threatens structural shear limits, or breaches clearance buffers, the enforcer automatically clamps the actuation setpoint to the boundary of the safe set or initiates an emergency stop. Subordinate all manual authority to a hardware-timed watchdog lease sized to the active mode's stopping reserve, guaranteeing that lease expiration automatically executes a deterministic brake or hold sequence without software intervention.

:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-verifier-flood-pitfall
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FORGED PACKETS QUEUED AHEAD OF A GENUINE VETO
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-fallacies-pitfalls, the verifier-flooding
# │          pitfall.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that authentication alone leaves an availability hazard:
# │          forged packets that the verifier must reject still spend its time.
# │ Show:    The signature verification time per packet; the fewest forged
# │          signed takeover requests queued ahead of a genuine veto that push
# │          its admission past T_latest at the aisle speed; the admission time
# │          they cause and the arrival rate they need; the same count for
# │          MAC-only frames.
# │ How:     Serial verification on the permission processor, each signed
# │          packet taking t_sig of InterventionAuthBudget; the genuine veto
# │          finishes after (n + 1) verifications; the forgeries must arrive
# │          within that interval.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, second, hertz
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_latency, fmt_count, check

class InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall:
    """Forged takeover packets that delay a genuine veto past T_latest."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_verify = InterventionAuthBudget.t_sig  # category: derived (sourced cycles / MCU clock)
    t_mac = InterventionAuthBudget.t_mac  # category: derived
    t_latest = InterventionTimeoutBudget.t_latest  # category: derived

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Fewest forged packets n with (n + 1) * t_verify > t_latest.
    n_forged = math.floor((t_latest / t_verify).to("").magnitude)
    t_admit = ((n_forged + 1) * t_verify).to(millisecond)
    # Whole packets per second the forger must sustain, rounded up.
    arrival_rate = math.ceil((n_forged / t_admit).to(1 / second).magnitude)
    n_forged_mac = math.floor((t_latest / t_mac).to("").magnitude)
    # The same count once the allocated Delta_da of @sec-placement-dispatch-admission is charged.
    n_forged_da = math.floor((InterventionAdmissionAllocation.left_aisle / t_verify).to("").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_forged == 55, f"forged packets that push the veto past T_latest: {n_forged}")
    check(t_admit > t_latest, "The queued forgeries must push the veto past T_latest.")
    check(n_forged * t_verify <= t_latest, "One fewer forgery must still let the veto fit.")
    check(n_forged_mac > 100 * n_forged, "A MAC-only flood needs far more frames than a signature flood.")
    check(n_forged_da == 20, f"forged packets once Delta_da is charged: {n_forged_da}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_verify_str = fmt_latency(t_verify, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_latest_str = fmt_latency(t_latest, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    t_admit_str = fmt_latency(t_admit, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    n_forged_str = fmt_count(n_forged)
    arrival_rate_str = fmt_int(arrival_rate)
    n_forged_mac_str = fmt_count(n_forged_mac)
    n_forged_da_str = fmt_count(n_forged_da)
    left_da_str = fmt_latency(InterventionAdmissionAllocation.left_aisle, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Relying on cryptographic authentication without rate limiting the traffic that reaches the verifier.*

Cryptographic authentication guarantees message authenticity and integrity, but it introduces an asymmetric computation cost that an adversary or a misbehaving transceiver can exploit to starve real-time processing. Suppose an admission controller validates incoming signed remote takeover requests (@sec-intervention-authenticating-intervention) using an embedded microcontroller that requires `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.t_verify_str` to verify each Ed25519 digital signature\index{Authentication!signature verification}. Malformed inputs may be rejected cheaply, but well-formed invalid signatures can still reach the expensive verification path. The following queue model charges every such request the stated verification time.

If a malfunctioning or compromised device on the network link\index{Network!availability} floods the interface with bogus signed `manual_drive` packets, as few as `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.n_forged_str` forged requests queued ahead of a critical `veto_path` message from a remote supervisor will delay its verification to `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.t_admit_str`. At aisle speed, this delay exceeds the fallback deadline $\FallbackDeadline$ of `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.t_latest_str`. When charging the allocated downstream admission delay $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$, the usable admission margin shrinks to `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.left_da_str`, meaning just `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.n_forged_da_str` forged packets suffice to cause a deadline violation. Sustaining this denial-of-service attack requires an injection rate of only `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.arrival_rate_str` packets per second, a trivial load for even a low-bandwidth industrial wireless channel.

Substituting symmetric MACs shifts the computational bottleneck to the network transceiver without eliminating the underlying vulnerability. Validating a MAC requires far fewer cycles, so roughly `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.n_forged_mac_str` forged frames within the same window are needed to induce a miss, yet the queue remains susceptible to line-rate saturating traffic. The robot's independently wired protective stops and hardware lease timers must never share queues with network ingress. Those local safety channels must remain fully operational even when the cryptographic verifier is saturated. To protect real-time responsiveness, the ingestion pipeline must deploy hardware mailbox filters and per-source rate limiters\index{Network!rate limiting} ahead of the verification queue, and safety qualification tests must evaluate worst-case intervention latency under full adversarial packet inundation.

**Cryptographic authentication protects command integrity but introduces an asymmetric availability risk, because an admission verifier spends finite compute cycles rejecting forged traffic before it can service critical safety messages.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** Deploy hardware mailbox filtering and per-source token-bucket rate limiters[^fn-token-bucket-limiter] on the fieldbus interface prior to the software verification queue. In addition, route emergency protective stops and fail-safe interlocks through dedicated, hardwired electrical circuits that bypass digital networking and cryptographic parsing entirely.

[^fn-token-bucket-limiter]: **Token Bucket**\index{Token bucket!verifier protection}: A limiter holds up to $\TokenBucketDepth$ tokens, refills at rate $\TokenBucketRefillRate$, and admits a packet only by spending a token, so a source may burst $\TokenBucketDepth$ packets but never sustain more than $\TokenBucketRefillRate$. Placed before the verifier, it bounds the forged signatures that can arrive within $\FallbackDeadline$ at $\TokenBucketDepth + \TokenBucketRefillRate\,\FallbackDeadline$. For the single-source queue modeled here, keeping that bound below the `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.n_forged_str` forgeries that push a genuine veto past its deadline, or `{python} InterventionVerifierFloodPitfall.n_forged_da_str` once $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ is charged, sizes $\TokenBucketDepth$ and $\TokenBucketRefillRate$ from the stopping budget rather than from link capacity. A deployed ingress must also bound aggregate traffic across sources, include already queued work and legitimate traffic, and prevent forged source identifiers from bypassing those limits.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Training directly on raw human intervention logs captures expert demonstrations.*

Training on raw intervention logs commits the learner-action contamination of @sec-data-intervention-recovery. The raw telemetry of a rescued episode is not a continuous expert demonstration\index{Imitation learning!expert demonstration}. It stitches the policy's diverging trajectory to the operator's reaction latency, the corrective jerks as the operator regains situational awareness, and the overshoots before stabilization, and a policy cloned from it reproduces the oscillations that made the takeover necessary.

The methods in @tbl-14-intervention-learning require attribution of who generated each state-action pair and a declared interpretation of the sample as a target, a weight, or a reward. Neither a coarse session-level takeover timestamp nor an active manual authority bit guarantees that recorded telemetry is fit for policy training. This chapter's conservative direct-imitation policy segments intervention trajectories into distinct causal regimes and masks transitional dynamics; the alternative objectives in @tbl-14-intervention-learning retain some early corrections.

**Unsegmented intervention telemetry records human cognitive lag and abrupt corrective overshoots; naively cloning these trajectories trains policies to reproduce the instability that triggered the takeover.**

**Architect's countermeasure:** For this chapter's conservative direct-imitation corpus, apply causal intervention masking (@eq-intervention-causal-masking-loss), taking the interval boundaries from the commit, blend-end, and stabilization timestamps on the safety microcontroller's monotonic hardware clock. Only Interval 4, validated post-stabilization guidance, trains as a human demonstration ($\CausalInterventionMask(\TimeInstant)=1$); Interval 1 drift states train only under an automated expert's labels, and everything else stays in the record for forensics.

:::

## Summary {#sec-intervention-summary}

```{python}
#| label: calc-intervention-summary-waiting
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WAITING BUDGET FOR THE SUMMARY AND TAKEAWAYS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-intervention-summary (first paragraph) and the chapter
# │          takeaways ("Clearance governs waiting").
# │
# │ Goal:    Restate the machine's handover deadline and takeover speeds.
# │ Show:    Spare margin and T_latest at the aisle speed; T_latest at the
# │          slow-down; the chosen slow-down and crawl speeds; the
# │          out-of-loop ceiling.
# │ How:     Finished stopping budget (jerk-limited resident stop, all
# │          overheads) from the WarehouseAisle scenario; ceilings by
# │          calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import meter, second, millimeter, millisecond
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_scurve_stop_distance,
    calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class InterventionSummaryWaiting:
    """Spare stopping margin spent as waiting time, and the takeover speeds it forces."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, AISLE.a_brake)["peak_jerk"]  # category: derived (stipulated jerk bound)
    overhead = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: illustrative / chosen
    t_in = AISLE.t_takeover_in_loop  # category: derived (sourced human + transport)
    t_ool = AISLE.t_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: derived (sourced human + transport)
    v_in = AISLE.v_takeover_in_loop  # category: chosen
    v_ool = AISLE.v_takeover_out_of_loop  # category: chosen
    t_latest_in = InterventionTimeoutBudget.t_latest_in  # category: derived

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    budget = (v * tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v, a_brake, j_brake) + overhead).to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
    t_latest = (spare / v).to(millisecond)
    ceil_in = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear,
        tau_delay + t_in,
```
